embedding_queries.text: For an essentially bounded measurable function on the unit interval, the L^p norm converges to the essential supremum norm as the exponent p tends to infinity.
On a finite measure space the L^p norm of a function is at most its essential supremum norm, because the integral of |f|^p is at most the essential supremum to the p times the measure of the space.

For a level below the essential supremum, the set where |f| exceeds the level has positive measure, so restricting the integral to that set gives a lower bound on the L^p norm by the level times the measure of the set to the power 1/p.
For a positive real number t, t to the power 1/p tends to 1 as p tends to infinity.
It suffices to prove the lower bound at one exponent, since on a probability space the L^p norm is monotone in the exponent, so the bound holds for all larger exponents.
The upper bound on the limsup and the lower bound on the liminf squeeze the L^p norms to the essential supremum norm.
